doc: Distance, walk-time and bearing rules. ADR-008's honesty applies to geography as much as to time: straight-line distance is an approximation, so metres are rounded to the nearest 10 and walk time to a whole minute, and nothing here pretends to be a road distance. Two conventions specific to this file: (1) the four float-returning groups compare with a `tolerance` in the same unit as the value, because no two languages' trigonometry libraries agree to the last bit — a port must assert |actual - expected| <= tolerance, NOT equality; (2) every rounding in this file is HALF-AWAY-FROM-ZERO on positives (JS `Math.round`, Swift `rounded()`, Kotlin `Math.round`). It is NOT banker's rounding: Kotlin's `Math.rint`, Python's `round()` and .NET's `Math.Round` default to half-to-even and will disagree on the .5 cases, which are called out individually below.

haversineMeters.doc: Great-circle distance between two WGS84 points, in metres, on a sphere of mean radius 6 371 008.8 m (the WGS84 authalic radius — a port must use the same constant or every figure drifts). Compare within `tolerance`.

cases.note: Across Victoria Harbour. About 2.35 km straight line; the real walk is a tunnel or a ferry, which is exactly why this is only ever shown as an approximation.
Tolerance 0: this must be exact, not near-zero. A port whose formula loses precision at zero would show a rider standing at the pole a non-zero distance.

The scale that matters most: two kerbs of the same interchange, ~68 m apart. ADR-042 clustering lives at this scale, so a port that is accurate over kilometres but sloppy over tens of metres breaks place merging rather than distance labels.
A scale-check independent of Hong Kong: one degree of latitude on this sphere. Equal to one degree of longitude at the equator, which catches a lat/lng transposition.

Half the sphere's circumference. The formula clamps the argument of asin to 1, so floating-point error just past the antipode yields the maximum distance rather than NaN. A port that omits the clamp returns NaN here on some inputs and the distance column silently blanks.

routeDistanceM.doc: Total straight-line length of an ordered path — the sum of great-circle hops. Used as an APPROXIMATE bus-route distance from its stop coordinates, because HK open data carries no route polylines. It therefore UNDER-counts: a bus follows curving roads, not straight hops between stops. Only ever shown as an explicit estimate (ADR-008/ADR-044).

cases.note: One stop is not a journey. Guards the loop's first iteration, which has no predecessor.
2349.0794 + 2297.6258. Proves the hops are summed consecutively rather than measured origin-to-terminus, which would give a much shorter figure for any route that curves back.
The origin and terminus coincide, as on a circular route. Straight-line displacement is zero but the path length is not — the row that catches a port measuring first-to-last.

walkMinutes.doc: Estimated walking minutes for a straight-line distance at 80 m/min (~4.8 km/h), rounded to a whole minute with a floor of 1. The floor exists because '0 min walk' is not information.

cases.note: Standing at the pole still reads '1 min walk'. Never 0.
40 m is exactly 0.5 min. Half-away-from-zero gives 1; the floor would give 1 anyway, so this row is only a partial discriminator — see the 200 m row for the real one.
THE ROUNDING-MODE ROW. 200 m is exactly 2.5 min. Half-away-from-zero gives 3. Banker's rounding (Kotlin Math.rint, Python round, .NET default) gives 2 and this row goes red — which is the point.

formatDistance.doc: Human distance. Under 1 km: metres rounded to the nearest 10, no space before the unit ('200m'). At or above 1 km: one decimal ('1.2km'). Unit symbols are locale-neutral, so this takes no locale. The tight spacing is deliberate — this is a glanceable label, not prose.

cases.note: Rounding to the nearest 10 means 4 m shows '0m'. Acceptable: the rider is standing at the stop.
Half-away-from-zero on the tens.

DEFECT. 995 m is below the 1 000 m branch, so it takes the metres path, and rounding to the nearest 10 lands on 1000 — the label reads '1000m' where it should read '1.0km'. Affects 995-999 m, i.e. one metre in every 200 shown. Cosmetic but visibly inconsistent next to a neighbouring stop's '1.0km'. Recorded so all platforms agree while it stands; the fix is to compare the ROUNDED metres against 1000, and it must land everywhere at once.

The far end of the same defect: 999 m also prints '1000m' rather than '1.0km'. Two rows because the range 995-999 is what the fix must cover, and a single row invites a port to special-case one value. Both become '1.0km' when the rounded metres are compared against 1000.
The first value on the km branch. One decimal is mandatory, so '1.0km' not '1km'.
1.25 km. Half-away-from-zero on the first decimal gives '1.3km'.

formatWalk.doc: Localized walk estimate for a single distance. The locale selects only the unit phrase; the figure is not localized. Note the English form has a space ('2 min walk') where formatDistance has none — the two labels sit next to each other and this asymmetry is intentional.

formatWalkRange.doc: Localized walk estimate across a RANGE of distances — the multi-pole place of ADR-042, where the poles of one place sit different walks away and quoting a single figure would be a guess about which kerb the rider wants. Collapses to one figure when the poles round to the same minute (never '4–4'), and is order-independent, so a caller may pass the two bounds either way round. The separator is U+2013 EN DASH with NO surrounding spaces — unlike formatHeadway, which spaces it. Both forms are deliberate and a port must not unify them.

cases.note: NAMED BOUNDARY ROW (a 4-member place). Clustering has been N-member since ADR-042, so the interesting case is not a pair. A four-pole interchange with member walks of 320 m / 350 m / 410 m / 480 m reduces to 4 min and 6 min; the caller passes the extremes. A port that only ever handled two poles, or that averaged them, gets this wrong — and averaging would be the worse failure, because it invents a walk to a kerb that does not exist.
The same four-pole place with the bounds swapped. Must produce the identical label, not '6–4'.
A four-pole place whose members are 310 m / 320 m / 330 m / 350 m — all 4 min. Never '4–4 min walk'.
Two poles 10 m and 30 m away both floor to 1 min, so no range appears.

formatBearing.doc: Localized 8-point compass direction for a MEAN TRAVEL BEARING, snapped to the nearest octant. This is the cue that tells two same-named places apart — the NE kerb from the SW kerb of one landmark (ADR-042) — so the label is '-bound' (a direction of travel), not a plain compass point. The input is degrees in ANY range: negatives and values over 360 are normalized first, which matters because a mean of bearings can legitimately come out negative. Octant index = round(normalized / 45) mod 8, over the table [N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW].

cases.note: 22 deg is nearer N than NE.
22.5 deg is exactly between N and NE, i.e. round(0.5). Half-away-from-zero gives octant 1 (NE); half-to-even gives octant 0 (N). This row separates the two rounding modes.
337.5 deg rounds to octant 8, which is taken modulo 8 back to North. A port that indexes an 8-element table without the modulo reads out of bounds here — a crash, or an empty label.
-45 deg is 315 deg. A mean of bearings either side of north can come out negative, so this is reachable, not hypothetical. A port using a bare `%` on a negative gets a negative index.
Traditional and Simplified differ for the eastern octants (東 vs 东) and agree for the others.
